title: Genesis 38. The Cup of the Scandal.
edition: AID Genesis, Layer 1 (the steward's manuscript); narration: Kristin voice (public domain)
level_note: text follows the narration phrase by phrase
verse_numbers: none in this text; none shown
phrases: Genesis 38. The Cup of the Scandal.
At that time, Judah went down from his brothers.
The chapter is a detour.
The Joseph story pauses.
The camera follows Judah, the one who said sell him.
The brother who calculated profit from a human life now walks away from the family that taught him to calculate.
He went down,
the same descent word used for Joseph going down to Egypt.
Judah descends.
Not into a pit.
Not into a foreign land.
Away from his brothers.
Away from the covenant's household.
Into Canaanite life.
He turned aside to an Adullamite named Hirah.
There Judah saw the daughter of a certain Canaanite man named Shua.
He took her and went in to her.
Saw.
Took.
The same pattern.
Shechem saw Dinah and took her.
The sons of Jacob saw the city of Shechem and took it.
Now Judah sees a Canaanite woman and takes her.
The grabber pattern, see, take, consume, runs through every generation.
Judah, who sold his brother,
now marries into the people his father was told to avoid.
The same thing Esau did.
The same thing Isaac told Jacob not to do.
The covenant line was sent to Paddan-aram for wives.
Judah takes a Canaanite.
She bore Er.
She bore Onan.
She bore Shelah.
Three sons.
The man who sold his brother now has three sons of his own.
The Cup that was held by a man who betrayed his sibling is now held by a father of three.
Judah took a wife for Er, his firstborn.
Her name was Tamar.
Tamar.
A name that means palm tree.
The woman who will carry the covenant line through a scandal that the Book of Witness refuses to clean up.
She enters the story as a wife,
given to a firstborn by a father who chose her.
Er, Judah's firstborn, was wicked in the sight of the Lord.
And the Lord killed him.
No explanation.
No list of sins.
Just: he was wicked.
The Lord killed him.
The first son of the man who sold his brother is killed by God.
The Cup that was filled through a Canaanite marriage is now emptied by divine judgment.
Judah said to Onan:
Go in to your brother's wife and perform the duty of a husband's brother to her.
Raise up offspring for your brother.
The levirate duty.
A brother must raise seed for a dead brother.
The Cup of the family line must not be allowed to end.
The name must not be blotted out.
Onan knew the offspring would not be his.
So when he went in to his brother's wife,
he spilled his semen on the ground,
lest he should give offspring to his brother.
Onan refuses.
He takes the pleasure but withholds the purpose.
He goes in, but he will not give.
The same pattern that runs through the grabbers: take what you want,
withhold what you owe.
The Cup of the family line is denied by a man who will not let it pass through him to someone else.
The thing which he did was evil in the sight of the Lord.
And He killed him also.
Two sons dead.
Judah has one left, Shelah.
And Judah is afraid.
Then Judah said to Tamar his daughter-in-law:
Remain a widow in your father's house,
until Shelah my son is grown up, for he said:
Lest he also die like his brothers.
Judah withholds.
The man who said sell him now says wait.
The father who lost two sons fears losing a third.
But the text reveals his heart:
he had no intention of giving her.
The Cup is denied, not by wickedness, as with Er and Onan,
but by fear.
Judah is afraid that Tamar is the cause of death.
He treats her as dangerous.
He sends her away.
He keeps his last son away from her.
The promise of a future is withheld by a man who has seen too much death.
Tamar went and lived in her father's house.
She waits.
The woman who was given to a husband who died.
Given to a second husband who died.
Promised a third husband who was never sent.
She waits in her father's house, a widow without a name,
without a son, without a future.
The Cup that was supposed to fill through her has been stopped by three men:
one wicked, one selfish, one afraid.
After many days, Shua's daughter, the wife of Judah, died.
Judah was comforted and went up to his sheep shearers at Timnah,
he and his friend Hirah the Adullamite.
Judah's wife dies.
He is comforted.
He goes up to shear sheep.
The man who went down from his brothers now goes up to Timnah.
The movement continues, down, up, away.
The father who withheld his son from his daughter-in-law now goes about his business.
Life has moved on.
Tamar was told: Behold,
your father-in-law is going up to Timnah to shear his sheep.
She saw that Shelah was grown up,
and she had not been given to him as a wife.
She saw.
The recognition verb again.
Tamar sees what Judah does not want seen.
Shelah is grown.
The promise was not kept.
The Cup was denied.
And Tamar decides to act.
She took off her widow's garments and covered herself with a veil and wrapped herself and sat at the entrance to Enaim,
which is on the way to Timnah.
She changes her garments.
The first garment transition since Joseph was stripped of his coat.
Joseph's coat was taken from him.
Tamar's garments are removed by choice.
She takes off the clothes of waiting and puts on the clothes of action.
She veils herself, the same veil Rebekah wore when she saw Isaac.
But where Rebekah veiled herself in modesty before a groom,
Tamar veils herself in disguise before a father-in-law.
When Judah saw her, he thought she was a prostitute,
for she had covered her face.
He turned to her by the way and said: Come now,
let me come in to you,
for he did not know that she was his daughter-in-law.
He did not know.
The recognition fails again.
Isaac did not know Jacob.
Jacob did not know his sons' lie.
Now Judah does not know Tamar.
The recognition pattern,
the verb that has run through every deception in Genesis,
now falls on the one who sold his brother.
The deceiver is deceived.
The man who said sell him is now drawn into a deception he cannot see.
She said: What will you give me,
that you may come in to me?
He said: I will send you a young goat from the flock.
A goat.
Again.
The animal that has appeared at every deception.
Jacob used goatskins.
The brothers used a goat's blood.
Now Judah offers a goat as payment for sex.
The same animal, the same pattern, the same cup,
running through every deception in Genesis.
She said: Will you give me a pledge until you send it?
He said: What pledge will I give you?
She said: Your seal, your cord,
and your staff that is in your hand.
The seal.
The cord.
The staff.
Identity.
The things that mark Judah as Judah.
The signet that authorizes his word.
The cord that binds it to his body.
The staff that marks him as a shepherd and a patriarch.
He gives them away.
The same pattern as Jacob giving away his identity through goatskins,
but reversed.
Jacob took someone else's identity.
Judah gives away his own.
The man who sold his brother now gives himself away for a moment of pleasure.
He gave them to her.
He came in to her.
She conceived by him.
Then she arose and went away and put off her veil and put on the garments of her widowhood.
The disguise is removed.
The veil comes off.
The widow's clothes go back on.
The woman who acted has now returned to waiting.
But she carries something,
not just the seal and the cord and the staff.
She carries the covenant line in her womb.
Judah sent the young goat by the hand of his friend the Adullamite,
to receive the pledge from the woman's hand.
But he did not find her.
He asked the men of the place:
Where is the prostitute who was at Enaim by the road?
They said: There has been no prostitute here.
Judah said: Let her keep the things, lest we be shamed.
Behold, I sent this goat, and you have not found her.
Let her keep them.
Judah chooses silence over exposure.
The man who said bring her out and let her be burned will later discover that the woman he condemned is the woman he paid.
But for now,
he lets the seal and the cord and the staff go.
He trades his identity for anonymity.
The Cup that was held by a man who valued profit over people now lets his own identity disappear to avoid shame.
About three months later, Judah was told: Tamar,
your daughter-in-law has played the prostitute.
And moreover, she is with child by prostitution.
Judah said: Bring her out.
Let her be burned.
Bring her out.
Let her be burned.
The man who went to a veiled woman on a road now condemns a woman for prostitution.
The man who withheld his son now demands death for the woman he failed.
The Cup of judgment,
held by a man who does not see his own sin in the sentence he pronounces,
is about to be turned back on him.
When she was brought out, she sent to her father-in-law, saying:
I am with child by the man who owns these.
And she said: Please recognize whose these are.
The seal, the cord, and the staff.
Recognize..
The same word the brothers used when they brought the blood-stained coat to Jacob:
Recognize now whether this is your son's tunic or not.
The same word.
The same formula.
The brothers said to Jacob: recognize this.
Now Tamar says to Judah: recognize this.
The recognition pattern has gone full circle.
Jacob deceived Isaac with a goat.
The brothers deceived Jacob with a goat.
Now Tamar deceives Judah with a goat,
and a seal and a cord and a staff.
Three generations of deception.
Three goats.
Three recognitions.
Three vessels that were fooled by the same pattern.
And Judah recognized them.
And said: She is more righteous than I.
She is more righteous than I.
The first confession of personal sin in Scripture.
Not: I sinned.
Not: forgive me.
But: she is more righteous than I.
Judah sees himself.
The man who sold his brother.
Who left his family.
Who withheld his son.
Who went to a woman he thought was a prostitute.
Who condemned a woman for the very act he committed with her.
He sees.
And he speaks.
The Cup of the scandal holds this:
the covenant line goes through Tamar.
Through a woman who was denied justice by three men and took it by deception.
Through a father-in-law's sin.
Through a confession that names the other person as more righteous.
Because I did not give her to Shelah, my son,
and he knew her again no more.
He names the sin.
Not the prostitution.
Not the deception.
The withholding.
The thing he did not do.
The son he did not give.
The promise he did not keep.
Judah's confession is not about what he did,
it is about what he failed to do.
The Cup was not emptied by what was poured in.
It was emptied by what was held back.
In the time of her labor, behold, twins were in her womb.
When she labored, one put out a hand,
and the midwife took and tied a scarlet thread on his hand,
saying: This came out first.
But as he drew back his hand, behold, his brother came out.
Twins.
Again.
Another set of struggling twins.
Esau and Jacob struggled in the womb.
Now Perez and Zerah struggle in the birth canal.
The first puts out a hand, marked with scarlet.
Then draws back.
And the second breaks out first.
She said: How have you broken out?
What breach is upon you?
Therefore his name was called Perez, Breach.
Perez.
The breach.
The one who breaks through.
The covenant line goes through a breach,
through what should not have happened but did.
Through a scandal.
Through a woman who was denied and a man who confessed.
Through twins who struggled like their father and uncle struggled.
Through a hand that reached out first and drew back,
like Jacob reaching for Esau's heel.
Afterward, his brother came out,
who had the scarlet thread on his hand.
His name was called Zerah, Dawn, Rising.
Zerah.
The scarlet thread.
The one who was first but was not first.
The one marked before birth who arrived second.
The same pattern as Jacob and Esau, the younger surpassing the older.
The same oracle: the older shall serve the younger.
The same struggle.
The same Cup, carried through the breach, not through the expected line.
Perez is the ancestor of David.
The covenant line,
the line of kings that God promised Jacob at Bethel,
goes through Judah's confession, through Tamar's boldness, through a breach.
Through what was broken.
Through what was scandalous.
Through what should not have been but was.
The Cup of the scandal is not the Cup of the covenant's failure.
It is the Cup of the covenant's honesty.
The Book of Witness does not clean this up.
It does not skip Judah's sin.
It does not skip Tamar's deception.
It does not skip the death of two sons or the fear of a father or the burning judgment that was turned back on the judge.
It holds all of it.
The covenant travels through broken vessels.
Through scandals.
Through confessions.
Through breaches.
From Noah's tent to Lot's cave to Rebekah's deception to Jacob's goatskins to Judah's seal,
the Cup has always traveled through what is broken.
The promise has always been carried by people who are not clean.
The covenant has always gone through the breach,
not through the expected door, not through the proper channel,
but through the crack, through the scandal,
through the thing that should not have happened but did.
Perez.
The breach.
The covenant's door.
